row.basis: writing and recitation of Moses' memorial
row.note: God tells Moses to write the Amalek memory in a book and rehearse it to Joshua. It concretely joins the commentary's Mosaic sheets to revealed words preserved by oral recitation.

row.basis: Book of the Covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses takes a written covenant book and reads it to Israel; it supplies the page-to-hearing movement developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Moses finishes writing Torah in a book
row.note: Within Deuteronomy Moses completes a written law-book. It is the closest Hebrew Bible anchor for the commentary's naming of Mosaic sheets, without equating their contents.

row.basis: book placed as witness
row.note: The book is deposited beside the ark as a witness against a resistant people; this sharpens 87:18's appeal to old writing against present objection.

row.basis: tablet and scroll for future days
row.note: Isaiah's contested warning is deliberately written on tablet and scroll for future time. Its context explains why an insistently spoken warning can invoke an enduring document.

row.basis: plainly written vision on tablets
row.note: Habakkuk requires a vision to be legible to a reader on tablets, a material counterpart to the commentary's spread-out, visible sheets.

row.basis: vision's appointed end
row.note: The written vision awaits an appointed end and will prove true; it supplies a Jewish-scriptural analogue for the commentary's ta'wil as a word's eventual arrival.

row.basis: fading grass and enduring divine word
row.note: Isaiah contrasts perishing vegetation with God's word standing forever, matching the commentary's inference that an enduring word outlasts the near world.

row.basis: Book of the Law found
row.note: Hilkiah's recovery of a long-neglected law book makes an old written word newly heard in Judah, a concrete alternative to calling its demand a novelty.

row.basis: replacement scroll with former words
row.note: After the king burns Jeremiah's roll, a new scroll is ordered with all former words. It makes textual survival amid rejection a precise counterpart to old pages still speaking.

row.basis: word in mouth and heart
row.note: Torah is said to be near in mouth and heart for doing, not merely on an external object; this parallels the commentary's move from pages to memorized recitation.

row.basis: law written on hearts
row.note: Jeremiah relocates Torah from document to inward writing, a close Jewish analogue to the commentary's pages reappearing in a hearer's chest and voice.

row.basis: Ezekiel eats a scroll then speaks
row.note: Ezekiel receives and consumes a physical scroll before speaking. Against the commentary's claim that the Qur'anic messenger is given recitation rather than a sheet, the contrast marks two modes of prophetic embodiment.

row.basis: book of remembrance, fear, and name
row.note: The book records those who fear the Lord and esteem his name. It combines the commentary's unforgetting divine book with fear, name-remembrance, and worship.

row.basis: God's book and the sinner
row.note: God says the individual sinner will be blotted from his book, combining the commentary's divine record with its former-scroll rule of non-transferable guilt.

row.basis: each dies for own sin
row.note: Mosaic law forbids executing children or parents for one another's sin. It is a direct legal antecedent to the commentary's 'no bearer bears another burden.'

row.basis: neither son nor father bears guilt
row.note: Ezekiel states the same rule as a theological axiom, making the commentary's individual purification and accountability legible within a later Jewish prophetic debate.

row.basis: repaid according to work
row.note: Job's speaker says God returns a person's work to them; it corresponds precisely to the former-sheet sequence of effort seen and recompensed.

row.basis: court sits and books open
row.note: Daniel's throne vision opens books in the final court. It pairs the commentary's preserved book with an eschatological disclosure of human history.

row.basis: awakening to everlasting outcomes
row.note: Daniel raises the dead to everlasting life or abhorrence, giving explicit Hebrew Bible form to the commentary's insistence that the later life is the decisive enduring horizon.

row.basis: spirit returns to God
row.note: Ecclesiastes describes dust returning to earth and spirit returning to God, a concise counterpart to the commentary's 'the destination is to the Lord.'

row.basis: gain world and lose life
row.note: Jesus opposes gaining the whole world to losing one's life; this specifies the commentary's warning about preferring the near life over the better future.

row.basis: perishable food and food enduring
row.note: Jesus tells hearers to work for food that endures into eternal life, a close formal parallel to near, perishing provision versus a lasting destination.

row.basis: world passes and doer abides
row.note: 1 John explicitly contrasts the passing world and desire with the one doing God's will abiding forever, directly mirroring the temporal and enduring antithesis.

row.basis: each bears own load
row.note: Paul says each person will bear their own load, an especially close Christian parallel to the commentary's no-vicarious-burden formulation.

row.basis: own labor and own reward
row.note: Each worker receives a reward according to their own labor; this matches the commentary's link between personal striving and its later recompense.

row.basis: judgment according to deeds in body
row.note: Each person appears before Christ's tribunal to receive what was done in the body, joining individual agency to the final outcome stressed by the commentary.

row.basis: opened books and judgment by deeds
row.note: Revelation's dead are judged from opened books according to deeds. It makes the commentary's pages, personal effort, and final accounting one scene.

row.basis: wash yourselves and make yourselves clean
row.note: Isaiah uses reflexive cleansing commands before ethical reform. That makes a concrete Hebrew parallel to 87:14's self-purification rather than a generic purity theme.

row.basis: purifies self through future hope
row.note: 1 John links self-purification to hope in the appearing to come, closely joining the commentary's tazakka and its future horizon.

row.basis: prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and righteousness
row.note: Raphael commends prayer together with fasting, almsgiving, and righteousness. It gives a Jewish late-antique counterpart to the commentary's prayer-and-purification pair.

row.basis: almsgiving purges sin and saves from death
row.note: Tobit gives almsgiving an explicitly purgative and life-preserving effect, a precise Jewish comparison for purification expressed through giving.

row.basis: prayers and alms as memorial
row.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, directly pairing worship and giving like the commentary's surrounding prayer and purification.

row.basis: calling on the divine name and deliverance
row.note: Hebrew Joel says everyone calling on YHWH's name will escape. It provides a direct older-scriptural counterpart to remembering the Lord's name and praying.

row.basis: Pharaoh asks who YHWH is
row.note: Pharaoh refuses Moses after asking who YHWH is. This is the closest Hebrew Bible scene to the commentary's Pharaoh asking Moses about his Lord.

row.basis: former writings for present hope
row.note: Paul expressly says earlier writings were written for current instruction and hope, a Christian account of how an ancient corpus can address present hearers.

row.basis: fulfilling Law and Prophets
row.note: Jesus frames his mission as fulfillment rather than abolition of Law and Prophets. It is a Christian model of a later proclamation claiming continuity with earlier writings.

row.basis: Moses wrote about Jesus
row.note: Jesus appeals to Moses's writing as testimony about him. The verse is a focused Christian rereading of Mosaic text as witness to a later message.

row.basis: Law, Prophets, and Psalms fulfilled
row.note: Luke groups Moses, Prophets, and Psalms as writings whose contents must be fulfilled. It gives a canonical Christian version of old scripture carrying a later realization.

row.basis: good news beforehand to Abraham
row.note: Paul calls God's promise to Abraham a prior proclamation of the gospel. This is a particularly direct Christian expansion of the commentary's appeal to Abraham's earlier sheets.

row.basis: better heavenly country of the patriarchs
row.note: Hebrews identifies the patriarchs' desired country as better and heavenly, placing Abraham's line inside the commentary's better, enduring-afterlife contrast.

row.basis: Moses rejects Egypt's treasure for reward
row.note: Hebrews interprets Moses as valuing God's reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked to reward. It supplies a Christian Mosaic reading of worldly preference versus future recompense.

row.basis: Moses and Prophets versus a demanded sign
row.note: Abraham says those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection. It closely matches the commentary's claim that a further visible sign or sheet would not cure refusal.

row.basis: examining Scripture to test a spoken message
row.note: The Bereans test a newly preached word against the Scriptures daily. It gives a concrete reception practice for the commentary's assertion that a current utterance belongs with old writings.

row.basis: Moses read every Sabbath
row.note: Moses is publicly read in synagogues every Sabbath, showing how an ancient Mosaic text remains a voiced communal teaching rather than a mute archive.

row.basis: Isaiah scroll unrolled and read
row.note: Jesus receives, unrolls, and reads Isaiah's scroll in synagogue. The scene materializes the commentary's sheet, voice, and present hearer in one act.

row.basis: letter on hearts, not ink
row.note: Paul contrasts ink and stone with a Spirit-written letter on human hearts. This develops the same page-to-interior movement that the commentary draws from recitation.

row.basis: in the scroll of the book it is written of me
row.note: Hebrews places its Christological claim in a book-scroll formula, a deliberate Christian claim that a later vocation is already inscribed in earlier Scripture.

row.basis: Moses offers blotting from the book for Israel
row.note: Moses offers his own erasure from God's book for Israel's sin. In contrast to the commentary's non-transferable burden, it foregrounds intercession; the next verse returns judgment to each sinner.

row.basis: bearing one another's burdens
row.note: Paul commands bearing one another's burdens. Against Galatians 6:5's individual load and the commentary's judicial rule, this preserves a social-ethical sense of shared burden rather than transferred guilt.

row.basis: God cleanses by sprinkling
row.note: Ezekiel promises God will sprinkle clean water and cleanse Israel. This is a deliberate counterweight to the commentary's reflexive tazakka, locating cleansing chiefly in divine action.

row.basis: new covenant with Israel and Judah
row.note: Jeremiah explicitly announces a new covenant with Israel and Judah. Alongside 87:18's denial that teaching is a mere novelty, it offers a different scriptural account in which newness and continuity coexist.

row.basis: a prophet charged with speaking falsehood
row.note: Judean leaders tell Jeremiah he is speaking falsely. The concrete charge against a prophet's command parallels the commentary's anticipated claim that a revelation is the speaker's invention.

row.basis: learning without formal study
row.note: Jesus's hearers ask how he has learning without formal study. It gives a Christian analogue to the commentary's attention to a messenger who has not learned ancient pages by ordinary reading.

row.basis: Arabic akhira and Hebrew aḥarit
row.note: Hebrew aḥarit, 'end' or 'latter outcome,' is a cognate of the commentary's Arabic akhira. Isaiah's God declares the aḥarit from the beginning, a lexical and structural companion to first pages carrying their end.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human use
row.note: God causes grass for cattle and vegetation for human use. It closely matches the Taha–A'la comparison in the commentary: rain-grown plants, grazing animals, and provision after creation.

row.basis: all in tombs will hear
row.note: Jesus says all in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a Christian answer to the commentary's question about the first generations: they too are gathered for a future day.

row.basis: Torah given scroll by scroll
row.note: The Talmud debates whether Torah was given scroll by scroll or as a completed whole. That reception history directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that suhuf are discrete sheets rather than a bound codex.

row.basis: Moses's chain of transmission
row.note: Mishnah Avot presents Moses handing Torah through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly. It makes the commentary's image of first writing leading later hearers into an explicit Jewish chain.

row.basis: Abraham kept Torah before Sinai
row.note: Rabbinic tradition says Abraham kept the whole Torah, even an eruv tavshilin. It offers a Jewish interpretive way to imagine Abraham as bearer of pre-Mosaic teaching, without positing extant Abrahamic pages.

row.basis: law burned and knowledge lost
row.note: Ezra says the law has been burned so no one knows what God has done or will do. It gives a Jewish counter-history to the commentary's confidence that former pages remain available.

row.basis: twenty-four books made public
row.note: After dictation restores books, Ezra is told to publish the first twenty-four for all readers. This furnishes a Jewish analogue to old written teaching made public again.

row.basis: seventy books reserved for the wise
row.note: Ezra is told to reserve seventy books for the wise. This contrasts with the commentary's rhetorical picture of an openly sufficient earlier warning, while concretely extending its concern with pages hidden or disclosed.

row.basis: Old and New Testaments mutually disclose
row.note: Augustine's formula that the New lies hidden in the Old and the Old becomes manifest in the New formalizes a Christian reading of the continuity claim, without making the Qur'anic text its premise.

row.basis: hope full of immortality
row.note: Wisdom gives the righteous, though punished in human sight, a hope full of immortality. It is a Hellenistic Jewish articulation of the enduring future that the commentary sets over the near life.

row.basis: write the song, teach it, put it in mouths
row.note: God commands Moses to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths. It is a particularly exact Mosaic pairing of written witness, recitation, memory, and a resistant audience.

row.basis: king writes a Torah copy in a book
row.note: The king must write his own Torah copy from the priestly exemplar. This develops the commentary's concern with sheets as authoritative, transmissible written objects rather than an abstract antiquity.

row.basis: daily reading of the written Torah
row.note: The king reads the written Torah all his life in order to fear God and obey. It supplies an older scriptural account of a page becoming enduring ethical formation.

row.basis: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
row.note: Joshua's law-book must not leave his mouth but be meditated on and done. It closely joins the commentary's page, oral recitation, internal remembering, and conduct.

row.basis: prophetic words dictated onto a scroll
row.note: Baruch writes on a scroll all the words Jeremiah has spoken from the prophet's mouth. It gives a precise Hebrew Bible instance of oral revelation becoming separate written pages.

row.basis: seek and read the book of YHWH
row.note: Isaiah orders hearers to seek and read YHWH's book, whose announced creatures are not missing. It makes a preserved prior writing an available public check on a present claim.

row.basis: word accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The word sent from God's mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose. It supplies a close biblical analogue to the commentary's ta'wil: a spoken word reaches the end it declares.

row.basis: the dead live and awake
row.note: Isaiah calls the dead to live and those in dust to awake. It gives a direct Hebrew Bible answer to the commentary's concern for the first generations and their future gathering.

row.basis: bread and every word from God's mouth
row.note: Manna teaches that life is not sustained by bread alone but by every word from God. This is a concrete predecessor to preferring a lasting divine word over immediate provision.

row.basis: heard word received as God's, not human
row.note: Paul commends hearers for receiving the proclaimed word as God's rather than a human word. It directly addresses the commentary's anticipated charge that revelation is merely the speaker's own speech.

row.basis: message received through revelation, not human teaching
row.note: Paul says he neither received nor learned his gospel from a human source but through revelation. This provides a Christian analogue to the commentary's contrast between ordinary textual learning and revealed recitation.

row.basis: prophecy not from human will
row.note: Prophecy is said not to arise from human will, but from people speaking from God while carried by the Holy Spirit. It gives an explicit Christian response to the invention accusation developed around 87:18.

row.basis: Deuteronomy's word in mouth and heart reapplied
row.note: Paul cites the Torah's word as near in mouth and heart and identifies it with the proclaimed word of faith. This is a direct Christian rereading of the oral-and-inward Torah motif beside the commentary's recited former pages.

row.basis: Scripture fulfilled in the hearers' hearing
row.note: After reading Isaiah's scroll, Jesus says the Scripture is fulfilled today in the audience's hearing. It closely models the commentary's claim that an old written word becomes present through a current recitation.

row.basis: seen things temporary, unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul explicitly contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal. It is a direct Christian formulation of the commentary's near-world versus enduring-future opposition.

row.basis: no lasting city here, city to come
row.note: Hebrews denies that believers have a lasting city here and directs them toward the one to come. This gives a concrete social image to the commentary's preference for the abiding later life.

row.basis: cleansing ourselves in fear of God
row.note: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and complete holiness in fear of God. The reflexive language and fear make it a close counterpart to the commentary's tazakka and yahsha.

row.basis: washing sins while calling the name
row.note: Paul is told to wash away sins while calling on the Lord's name. It directly binds purification to name-invocation, two elements the commentary brings together around 87:14-15.

row.basis: enduring word identified with preached good news
row.note: The Lord's word remains forever, and the letter identifies that enduring word with the good news preached to its hearers. It is a Christian reception of the commentary's old-word-to-present-voice claim.

row.basis: one reads, others hear, all keep written prophecy
row.note: Revelation blesses the reader, the hearers, and those who keep a written prophecy. The verse gives a compact Christian scene in which a text, voiced reading, and ethical response remain inseparable.

row.basis: this world as vestibule before the world to come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the World to Come and urges preparation for entry. It provides a concise rabbinic analogue to the commentary's near life ordered toward a lasting later reality.

row.basis: a share in the world to come
row.note: The Mishnah opens its judgment discussion by assigning Israel a share in the World to Come while naming exclusions. It supplies a Jewish communal and ethical frame for the commentary's decisive future outcome.

row.basis: World to Come beyond eating and drinking
row.note: The Talmud portrays the World to Come as beyond eating and drinking, with the righteous enjoying the divine presence. It sharpens the commentary's contrast between immediate material life and enduring eschatological enjoyment.

row.basis: deeds with fruit now and principal in the world to come
row.note: The Mishnah distinguishes the present fruit of certain deeds from their enduring principal in the World to Come. This is a precise Jewish counterpart to present action receiving a later, fuller outcome.

row.basis: testimony bound and teaching sealed
row.note: Isaiah binds and seals testimony among disciples. It offers a counter-image to the commentary's open sheets: teaching is preserved, yet access is marked by a bounded circle of transmitters.

row.basis: visions from a prophet's own heart
row.note: Jeremiah warns against prophets who speak visions from their own hearts rather than YHWH's mouth. It supplies the Hebrew Bible's own criterion for the human-invention charge that 87:18 rhetorically rejects.

row.basis: present repentance and future bliss compared
row.note: Avot calls one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world greater than all the World to Come, then calls one hour of World-to-Come bliss greater than all worldly life. Its two-sided comparison complicates, yet productively parallels, the commentary's simple worldly-versus-lasting contrast.
